clinicalPearls: Flexible endoscopes generate an electronic video image from a CCD or CMOS chip at the tip, with operator tip-deflection controls, light delivery, and working channels for washing, suction, and accessory passage (Harrison 22e p.2465).

Upper endoscopy (EGD) is the best method for examining the upper GI mucosa and is superior to a barium upper-GI series for detecting gastric ulcers and flat lesions such as Barrett's esophagus, while also permitting directed biopsy and therapy (Harrison 22e p.2465).

Colonoscopy is the gold standard for imaging the colonic mucosa, reaching the cecum in over 95% of cases, with greater sensitivity than barium enema for colitis, polyps, and cancer; CT colonography rivals it for many polyps and cancers but is less sensitive for flat serrated lesions (Harrison 22e p.2465).

For obscure small-bowel bleeding, capsule endoscopy visualizes mucosa beyond the reach of a conventional endoscope but is purely diagnostic; push and balloon-assisted enteroscopy allow deeper intubation with biopsy and therapy (Harrison 22e p.2465-2466).

EUS provides the most accurate preoperative local staging of esophageal, pancreatic, and rectal malignancies but does not detect distant metastases beyond its imaging range; it also enables fine-needle aspiration/biopsy and a growing range of therapeutic drainage procedures (Harrison 22e p.2468).

Endoscopic stigmata of a peptic ulcer carry prognostic value: a clean-based ulcer has a low (3-5%) rebleeding risk, flat pigmented spots ~10%, adherent clot ~20%, a visible vessel ~40%, and active spurting ~90% (Harrison 22e p.2478-2479).

Over 90% of patients with melena bleed proximal to the ligament of Treitz and ~85% with hematochezia bleed from the colon, but massive hematochezia can reflect a brisk upper-GI source with rapid transit, warranting urgent upper endoscopy (Harrison 22e p.2476).

Severity of the initial hemorrhage is the most important indicator for urgent endoscopy; falling hematocrit and hemoglobin lag behind the clinical course and are unreliable gauges of acute blood loss (Harrison 22e p.2476).

Acute esophageal obstruction from food impaction or a foreign body is an endoscopic emergency; untreated it can lead to esophageal ulceration, ischemia, and perforation, and an underlying web, ring, or stricture is often present (Harrison 22e p.2484-2485).

In acute colonic pseudoobstruction (Ogilvie's), the risk of cecal perforation rises when cecal diameter exceeds 12 cm, prompting decompression with intravenous neostigmine or colonoscopy (Harrison 22e p.2487).

Charcot's triad (jaundice, abdominal pain, fever) is present in ~70% of ascending cholangitis; the addition of shock and confusion (Reynolds's pentad) signals high mortality and warrants urgent biliary drainage, typically by ERCP (Harrison 22e p.2489).

Long-standing GERD confers a roughly sixfold increased risk of Barrett's esophagus versus reflux of under one year; screening EGD should be considered after a chronic (>=10-year) GERD history even when symptoms are mild (Harrison 22e p.2490-2491).
harrison.pathophysiology: Gastrointestinal endoscopy is a diagnostic and therapeutic modality rather than a disease; it directly visualizes mucosal and luminal pathology and adjacent structures (via EUS) and provides access for tissue sampling and intervention. Many of the conditions it manages share a vascular or mechanical basis: peptic ulcers bleed when erosion exposes a submucosal vessel; a Dieulafoy's lesion is an abnormally large-caliber persistent artery running just beneath the epithelium that bleeds through a focal mucosal defect; a Mallory-Weiss tear is a mucosal rent at the gastroesophageal junction caused by retching/vomiting that can disrupt a submucosal arteriole; colonic diverticular bleeding arises from the nutrient artery at the base of a diverticulum; and vascular ectasias are flat mucosal vascular anomalies (e.g., GAVE/watermelon stomach) that cause slow blood loss. Variceal bleeding reflects portal hypertension. Obstructive syndromes (esophageal food impaction, gastric outlet obstruction, colonic obstruction/pseudoobstruction, biliary obstruction by stone) produce luminal blockage that endoscopy can relieve. Barrett's esophagus represents columnar metaplasia of distal esophageal squamous mucosa driven by chronic acid reflux and is a precursor to adenocarcinoma (Harrison 22e p.2464-2491).
additionalDifferentials: Melena: distinguish proximal upper-GI bleeding from slow right-colon or small-bowel sources, especially in older patients with slow colonic transit
Hematochezia: colonic source vs brisk upper-GI bleed with rapid transit
Dyspepsia: gastroesophageal reflux vs peptic ulcer disease vs nonulcer (functional) dyspepsia vs uncommon gastric/esophageal malignancy
Colonic dilatation: mechanical obstruction (e.g., malignancy, sigmoid volvulus) vs acute colonic pseudoobstruction
Diverticular hematochezia: exclude vascular ectasias, colitis, and colon cancer before attributing bleeding to a diverticulum
additionalInvestigations: 24-hour ambulatory pH and impedance monitoring as the most sensitive test for GERD, capturing nonerosive reflux disease that endoscopy may miss
MRCP and EUS for bile duct stones (>90% accurate), reserving ERCP for cases needing therapy or high pretest probability
Noninvasive H. pylori testing (serology for past/current infection; urea breath test and stool antigen for current infection) before or in lieu of endoscopy in younger patients without alarm features

Capsule endoscopy as the typical next test after negative upper and lower endoscopy in suspected small-bowel bleeding (diagnostic yield ~55%), with a patency capsule beforehand if stricture risk exists

Plain abdominal radiography (and water-soluble contrast enema or CT) to assess colonic dilatation and differentiate obstruction from pseudoobstruction; neck/chest radiographs before endoscopy for esophageal obstruction with fever, >=24-h impaction, or sharp object
redFlags: Resting hypotension, orthostatic vital-sign change, repeated hematemesis, bloody nasogastric aspirate not clearing with lavage, or transfusion requirement — consider urgent endoscopy within 12-24 h
Dyspepsia or reflux with alarm features (weight loss, obstructive symptoms, dysphagia, GI bleeding, iron-deficiency anemia) — perform endoscopy at the outset
Esophageal food/foreign-body impaction with hypersalivation and inability to swallow water — endoscopic emergency
Reynolds's pentad (Charcot's triad plus shock and confusion) in ascending cholangitis — urgent biliary drainage
Cecal diameter exceeding 12 cm in colonic pseudoobstruction — impending perforation
Age >70, cirrhosis, coagulopathy, or respiratory/renal failure with GI bleeding — higher rebleeding risk warranting prompt evaluation
harrison.prognosis: Outcomes depend on the underlying condition and endoscopic findings. Most GI bleeding stops spontaneously. Endoscopic therapy of high-risk peptic ulcer stigmata lowers rebleeding to about 5-10%. Endoscopic variceal ligation controls acute esophageal variceal hemorrhage in up to 90% of patients, though chronic eradication therapy prevents long-term rebleeding in only ~50%. A clean-based ulcer carries a low (3-5%) rebleeding risk, permitting early discharge of suitable patients. Post-ERCP pancreatitis is usually mild and self-limited but can be severe. Delayed biliary drainage in ascending cholangitis increases morbidity and mortality (Harrison 22e p.2464-2491).
pitfalls: Relying on hematocrit/hemoglobin to gauge acute bleeding — these lag behind the clinical course
Assuming melena always means an upper-GI source or hematochezia always a colonic source — exceptions occur with transit-dependent presentations
Performing ERCP indiscriminately in gallstone pancreatitis — only ~20% retain an ampullary/common-bile-duct stone, and initial MRCP/EUS reduces unnecessary ERCP and its adverse events
Using endoscopy to diagnose nonerosive reflux disease — it will miss symptomatic reflux without esophagitis
Treating a Mallory-Weiss tear bearing a nonbleeding sentinel clot like a peptic ulcer — unlike ulcers, such tears rarely rebleed and need no endoscopic therapy
Relying on epinephrine injection alone for ulcer hemostasis — it slows bleeding but is not definitive monotherapy
Obtaining radiographic contrast studies before endoscopy in suspected esophageal obstruction — contrast interferes with the subsequent endoscopic procedure
Proceeding to endoscopy in marked coagulopathy or thrombocytopenia without correction — hemostatic techniques are limited and correction may itself resolve bleeding
harrison.severityClassification: Peptic ulcer rebleeding risk by endoscopic stigmata: clean base 3-5%; flat pigmented spots ~10%; adherent clot ~20%; nonbleeding visible vessel ~40%; active spurting ~90% (Harrison 22e p.2478-2479). Procedural adverse-event risk: bleeding/perforation under 1:1000 for diagnostic EGD, flexible sigmoidoscopy, and colonoscopy, rising to 0.5-5% with therapeutic maneuvers; ERCP carries ~5% pancreatitis risk (up to ~25% in young, anicteric patients with normal ducts) and ~1% post-sphincterotomy bleeding; PEG placement has a 10-15% adverse-event rate (Harrison 22e p.2473-2474).
management: Deliver endoscopic haemostasis for high-risk peptic ulcer stigmata such as a visible vessel, active spurting or adherent clot, using combination therapy with injection, thermal coagulation and clips
Perform endoscopic variceal band ligation to control acute oesophageal variceal haemorrhage
Ablate bleeding vascular ectasias endoscopically, typically with argon plasma coagulation
Undertake diagnostic and therapeutic tissue sampling, polypectomy and endoscopic mucosal resection at colonoscopy
Use capsule endoscopy and balloon-assisted enteroscopy for obscure small-bowel bleeding, preceded by a patency capsule where stricture risk exists
Employ endoscopic ultrasound for local staging of oesophageal, pancreatic and rectal tumours and for guided fine-needle aspiration and drainage
Attend to peri-procedural safety with sedation monitoring, review of antithrombotic therapy and correction of coagulopathy before intervention
